<reason>B built the stronger comparative case: continuing retail barriers can prevent dependence rather than merely displace existing demand, while conventional controls remain available. B directly answered the proxy-purchasing and enforcement questions, acknowledging loopholes and costs. A raised meaningful equality and diversion objections, but repeatedly treated expanding barred cohorts as expanding tobacco demand and overstated the collapse of enforcement legitimacy. B better justified the transitional purchasing inequality and explained why imperfect compliance need not defeat prevention.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A effectively challenged the assumption that fewer legal buyers necessarily means less diversion. B conceded that point, then distinguished possible intermediaries from dependable retail access and barred adults from inevitable smokers. Its closing observation that the forty-year-old “has a history” crystallized the prevention mechanism; A’s final appeal to nearby suppliers did not resolve it.</best_rebuttal>
